patterns.comment: Frontmatter open fence. The IntelliJ TextMate engine treats the document-start anchor `\A` like line-start `^`, so a `\A`-anchored bare `---` would also fire mid-document and swallow the rest of the file as frontmatter. To restore document-start semantics in a line-based engine, the open fence requires a typed format token (`---json`, `--- toml`, ...): a lone `---` line never triggers frontmatter and is left to the thematic-break rule (which runs first). A bare `---` open fence is therefore highlighted as a thematic break, matching the spec note that a bare `---` is frontmatter only when a closing `---` exists ahead -- a closer lookahead a line-based grammar cannot perform.
patterns.name: meta.frontmatter.carve

patterns.comment: A standalone line of three or more `-`, `*`, or `_` (optionally followed by trailing whitespace) is a thematic break. Listed before #frontmatter so a lone `---` line is claimed here rather than mis-detected as a frontmatter open fence (see #frontmatter).
patterns.name: meta.separator.thematic-break.carve
comment.block.carve
patterns.comment:
A %%% fence line is a delimiter plus an insignificant tail (spec PART 9 section 28): only the leading run of % is structural, so `%%% TODO` opens and `%%% end` closes. %%% carries no info string - a raw passthrough block is a CODE fence with an =FORMAT info string - so `%%% html` is a comment. The end backreference matches the opener width exactly, so %%%% nests %%%. AN UNCLOSED FENCE GREYS OUT THE REST OF THE DOCUMENT HERE, AND THE ENGINE DOES NOT - it degrades the opener to a line comment and hides nothing, so `%%%` / `body` renders `

body

` (markup-carve/intellij-carve#81). It cannot be fixed in this rule and the reason is worth writing down once, because the fix looks available and is not. The engine's rule is NOT LOCAL: whether this line is a fence or a line comment depends on whether a closer appears LATER, and a `begin` is matched against ONE LINE. Measured - a begin of `^\s*(%{3,})[^\n]*$(?=[\s\S]*?^\s*\1(?!%))` opens the fence on NEITHER a closed nor an unclosed document, because the lookahead never sees past the current line. NOR IS THERE A SAFE EARLY BOUNDARY to approximate it with, which is the other thing that looks available: `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` and `#comment-fence-on-quote-marker-line` each bound their runaway to the CONTAINER they sit in, and a top-level fence has none. Every shorter boundary cuts a legitimate fence in half - a body may span a blank line, may sit at column 0 under an indented opener, and may hold a heading and a nested code fence, while the closer need not share the opener's indent. All seven of those are pinned in CarveUnclosedFenceTest.aClosedCommentFenceHidesItsBody, so an attempt at the unclosed case fails there rather than shipping. All three TextMate grammars in the org carry this rule unchanged (carve-grammars `block_comment`, vscode-carve `#comments`); markup-carve/carve-grammars#260 fixed the same defect for highlight.js, which can read the whole document at once and so is not subject to any of this.

A DELIMITED INLINE COMMENT, `{% ... %}` (spec PART 9 section 21a, markup-carve/carve#1239). It hides its payload the way `%%` hides the rest of a line, so it is scoped WHOLE rather than letting the emphasis and attribute rules reach inside - `{% *not bold* %}` must not render a bold run. It sits after the code and literal inline rules so a `{%` inside a code span stays code, and before #trailing-comment so a `%%` in the payload does not open a second comment.
patterns.name: comment.block.inline.carve
markup.raw.block.fenced.code.carve
patterns.comment: AN UNCLOSED CODE FENCE RUNNING TO THE END OF THE DOCUMENT IS CORRECT and is not the comment fence's defect wearing a different delimiter: measured, the engine renders `` ```js `` / `code` / `` / `after` as ONE `<pre><code>` holding all of it, where an unclosed `%%%` degrades to a line comment instead (markup-carve/intellij-carve#81). Pinned in CarveUnclosedFenceTest.anUnclosedCodeFenceRunsToTheEndOfTheDocument so it is not bounded here by analogy.

patterns.name: markup.other.figure-group.carve
patterns.comment: Composite figure (PART 9 §4c, markup-carve/carve#1215; tracked as markup-carve/carve-grammars#222). The kind word `figure` is RESERVED among the `:::` types: a BARE opener - the fence, its separator, the word `figure`, and NOTHING else - is ONE figure of ordered panels, not the generic Tier-2 container, so it carries its own scope and this rule sits BEFORE `#divs` in the document pattern list. The `[ \t]*$` tail is the whole distinction: an opener carrying a quoted title or a `[label]` (`::: figure "T"`, `::: figure [g]`) does not match here at all and falls through to `#divs`, which is the generic container the clause says it stays - both spellings keep the exact scopes they had before this rule existed. THE SEPARATOR IS A SPACE RUN, never a tab (grammar.ebnf PART 7, MARKER SEPARATORS; corpus 254 renders `:::<TAB>note` as a paragraph), so it is spelled ` +` and NOT `[ \t]+`; a tab-separated `:::<TAB>figure` falls to `#divs` and reads exactly as it does today. Trailing whitespace after the kind word is insignificant and may be a tab. GROUPS DO NOT NEST: a bare `::: figure` at ANY depth inside an open group is a generic container (PART 9 §4c), which this rule gets for free by leaving itself out of its own `patterns` - `#divs` is a flat per-line `match` and recurses into no pattern list, so it cannot re-reach this rule from any depth. That is why there is no `divs-in-group` twin here, unlike carve-grammars' TextMate copy whose generic container is itself begin/end and therefore needs one. The closer backreferences the opener's colon run (`\1`), so it closes on an EXACT length match - PART 9 §12's colon-fence depth rule, and the reason a bare `:::` line inside a `:::: figure` group does not close it. A group left open at end of input closes there, like any container. THE GROUP CAPTION NEEDS NO RULE: it is an ordinary `^ ` line one line below the CLOSING fence, which the caption rule already claims at the document level. That claim is an OVER-APPROXIMATION and stays one - a `^ ` line after any other `:::` closer is ordinary paragraph content in the language, but it sits outside this rule's begin/end span, so no amount of container state here can tell the two apart. RESIDUAL: an opener carrying a bullet prefix (`- ::: figure`, corpus 114) is not matched here and falls to `#divs`; a line-based grammar has no list-item content column, and under-colouring the rare case is the side every block rule in this file already picks.

A div fence may open directly after a list marker (`- ::: note`), which is corpus-pinned (corpus 114). A BLOCK OPENER MAY SIT ON A LIST ITEM'S OWN MARKER LINE, and it opens the block there. Measured against the engine bundled in this plugin: `- # h`, `- [x] # h`, `1. # h` and `- - # h` all render the heading INSIDE the item, and `- ---`, `- [ ] ---`, `1. ---` render an `<hr>` inside it. `#block-quotes` and `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` already carry this shape for `>` and `%%%` (markup-carve/intellij-carve#73, #74). The rule here is the same shape for another line-anchored block opener, added with its siblings rather than one spelling at a time - this family has come back a spelling at a time in every grammar in the org. THE MARKER PREFIX IS CHARACTER FOR CHARACTER the one those two rules use, so all of them accept and reject the same marker forms: every separator is a literal space, and an ATTRIBUTE-GLUED marker (`-{#x} # h`) is not covered, because the block's width is not whitespace. The marker keeps its own list scopes and NOTHING ELSE - the block's scopes start past it, which is the split `#block-quotes` makes with its `contentName` and the one tree-sitter-carve models, with the block inside `list_item_content` beside the `list_marker_*` rather than over it. A `match` rule has no `contentName`, so the payload is a capture group carrying the block scope with its parts captured inside it. The prefix here was a SINGLE BULLET, so the one corpus spelling was covered and nothing else was: `- [ ] ::: d` and `1. ::: d` open a div inside the item in the engine and took no div scope at all. It stays OPTIONAL, because a div at column 0 is the ordinary case. The div scopes also moved off the marker and onto the payload, which is why corpus 114's golden changes: the bullet used to carry `markup.other.div.carve` and now carries the list scopes the rest of the family gives it. THE MARKER'S OWN SEPARATOR IS A LITERAL SPACE and any further indent before the payload is not: measured, `-\t# h` is a PARAGRAPH in the engine while `- \t# h` is a heading inside the item, because the tab there is content indent rather than the marker's separator. So the prefix admits spaces only and a `[ \t]*` sits between it and the payload.

GFM delimiter/alignment row: a whole line of only pipes, dashes, optional alignment colons, and whitespace (e.g. `|---|---|`, `|:---:|`). Gated by a full-row lookahead so an ordinary data cell that merely contains dashes is NOT mis-scoped. Note: TextMate rules are line-local and do not track table position, so a dash/colon-only row that is NOT the parser's second-row delimiter is also highlighted here -- rare and cosmetic.
patterns.name: markup.table.row.separator.carve

patterns.comment: Separator cell: leading/trailing alignment colons get a dedicated alignment scope; the dash run stays the separator punctuation.

A BLOCK QUOTE MAY OPEN ON A LIST ITEM'S OWN MARKER LINE (`- > x`, `1. > x`, `- - > x`, `- [ ] > x`), and it takes the rest of that line: carve-js at the pinned engine renders `

  • x

`. The rule below cannot reach it - it is anchored on ^ and the marker is in the way - so the line fell through to `#lists`, the marker was scoped and everything after it carried NO scope at all (markup-carve/intellij-carve#73). markup-carve/carve-grammars#246 left the shape out on the ground that a shape one grammar handles and two do not is drift; tree-sitter-carve models it now (markup-carve/tree-sitter-carve#218), so the reason has inverted. WHY THE MARKER IS MATCHED HERE RATHER THAN LEFT TO `#lists`. The sibling grammars reach this line with a \G-anchored rule that runs inside the list item's own container. This grammar has no container model - `#lists` is a line MATCH - so a \G rule would sit at the top level, where it fires after ANY match that ends on whitespace: `# > x` is a heading whose text is `> x`, and a top-level \G quote rule colours the `> x` there. Matching the marker line whole is what keeps the rule to the one shape. The marker keeps its own list scopes through the captures, and only the content past the `>` is `contentName`d as quote - which is tree-sitter-carve's split, the `block_quote` inside `list_item_content` beside the `list_marker_*` rather than over it. EVERY SEPARATOR IS A LITERAL SPACE: `-> q` and `- >x` are prose in the engine, and neither matches here. The ATTRIBUTE-GLUED marker (`-{#x} > q`) is not covered either - the block's width is not whitespace - so that line still falls through to `#lists` and behaves as it did. A TAB BETWEEN THE MARKER AND THE OPENER used to fall through: the opener was matched flush against the prefix, so `- \t> q` and `- \t%%%` took no scope even though the engine opens the block on both. The `[ \t]*` here is the same one the rest of the marker-line family carries. It is only the indent past the marker's own separator, which is still a literal space - `-\t> q` remains a paragraph.

Definition-list TERM line: a leading `::` marker. Only the marker is scoped (mirroring the single-colon definition rule below), so a trailing `%% comment` and any inline markup in the term still tokenize normally. Matched before the single-colon rule; `::` never collides with a `:::+` fenced div, which needs three colons. A BLOCK OPENER MAY SIT ON A LIST ITEM'S OWN MARKER LINE, and it opens the block there. Measured against the engine bundled in this plugin: `- # h`, `- [x] # h`, `1. # h` and `- - # h` all render the heading INSIDE the item, and `- ---`, `- [ ] ---`, `1. ---` render an `<hr>` inside it. `#block-quotes` and `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` already carry this shape for `>` and `%%%` (markup-carve/intellij-carve#73, #74). The rule here is the same shape for another line-anchored block opener, added with its siblings rather than one spelling at a time - this family has come back a spelling at a time in every grammar in the org. THE MARKER PREFIX IS CHARACTER FOR CHARACTER the one those two rules use, so all of them accept and reject the same marker forms: every separator is a literal space, and an ATTRIBUTE-GLUED marker (`-{#x} # h`) is not covered, because the block's width is not whitespace. The marker keeps its own list scopes and NOTHING ELSE - the block's scopes start past it, which is the split `#block-quotes` makes with its `contentName` and the one tree-sitter-carve models, with the block inside `list_item_content` beside the `list_marker_*` rather than over it. A `match` rule has no `contentName`, so the payload is a capture group carrying the block scope with its parts captured inside it. The payload here is the term marker itself: `- :: term`, `- [ ] :: term` and `1. :: term` all render a `<dl>` inside the item, so the marker prefix is admitted and is OPTIONAL. The single-colon DEFINITION line below is deliberately NOT given one - `- :  def` is ordinary item text in the engine, not a definition, so a prefix there would colour prose. THE MARKER'S OWN SEPARATOR IS A LITERAL SPACE and any further indent before the payload is not: measured, `-\t# h` is a PARAGRAPH in the engine while `- \t# h` is a heading inside the item, because the tab there is content indent rather than the marker's separator. So the prefix admits spaces only and a `[ \t]*` sits between it and the payload.
A lone `+` at the marker column is the list-continuation marker, not a bullet (`+` is never a bullet in Carve).
patterns.name: markup.list.continuation.carve
markup.list.unnumbered.carve
patterns.comment: A marker line may carry several markers (`- - A` opens two nested lists), so scope each one, not only the line-anchored first. A BULLET MAY BE GLUED TO AN ATTRIBUTE BLOCK, and then the required space comes after the block, not after the marker - so `-{#x} item` and `*{.c} item` went uncoloured on a line that IS a list item, while the ordered rule beside it already had the branch (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126). It is a LOOKAHEAD: consuming the block would make this rule own those characters, so the attribute rule could no longer scope them. KNOWN LIMITATION, shared with every Carve TextMate grammar: the checkbox after a glued block (`-{.c} [x] done`) is not scoped, because the task branch has none; the bullet is. THE PAYLOAD MUST BE VALID, not merely brace-delimited: an invalid one means the `{` is literal content and the line is prose. `-{+a+} text` (corpus 90-list-item-attributes-6) and `1.{2=v} text` are paragraphs, while `-{} item` and `-{not attrs} item` are list items. Identifiers are STRICT (PART 9 S14) and admit no colon, which is what carve-js does (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126).

Ordered markers use a trailing `.` or `)` only. A parenthesized `(1)` / `(a)` form is NOT a marker in Carve (it is too easily confused with prose), so no leading `(`. The BARE DOT is a marker on its own (carve#472): `.` continues an ordered sequence, and is the only marker allowed to drop its value. The lookahead admits a marker glued to an attribute block (`.{#x}`, `3.{#x k=v}`), which is how the corpus writes it - but the ATTRIBUTE FORM NEEDS CONTENT TOO: `1.{#x}` with nothing after the block is a paragraph, so the glued-block branch spells the block out in full rather than skipping it. A `\{[^}]*\}` run stops in the wrong place, because a quoted value may contain `}` and may escape its own quote, and `{title="a}b"} x` is a valid item (markup-carve/carve-grammars#85). A ROMAN RUN IS CASE-CONSISTENT: two classes, not one `[ivxlcdmIVXLCDM]`, which matched any mixture and coloured `Vim. text` and `Mix. text` as lists where carve-js renders paragraphs (markup-carve/carve-grammars#118). `mix.`, `civil.` and `did.` DO open lists, so the fix is the case split rather than rejecting multi-letter words. CarveMarkerScanner already uses the split form (#55). THE PAYLOAD MUST BE VALID, not merely brace-delimited: an invalid one means the `{` is literal content and the line is prose. `-{+a+} text` (corpus 90-list-item-attributes-6) and `1.{2=v} text` are paragraphs, while `-{} item` and `-{not attrs} item` are list items. Identifiers are STRICT (PART 9 S14) and admit no colon, which is what carve-js does (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126).
patterns.name: markup.list.numbered.carve
meta.link.inline.carve
patterns.comment: The optional title may be empty (`[x](u "")`) and may contain escaped quotes (`"ti\"tle"`), so the title run allows backslash escapes and zero characters.

patterns.name: meta.image.inline.carve
patterns.comment: The optional title may be empty and may contain escaped quotes; see the inline-link rule.

Inline footnote `^[content]` (core Carve). Its content is inline-parsed (spec `inline_footnote = '^[', inline_content, ']'`), so nested emphasis and code still tokenize. The `(?=$)` alternative in `end` bounds the span to one line so an unclosed `^[` cannot leak into following paragraphs.
patterns.name: meta.footnote.inline.carve

patterns.comment: Consume a backslash escape before the `end` check so `^[a \] b]` does not terminate at the escaped bracket.
patterns.name: constant.character.escape.carve

citations.comment: Citation group: a bracket whose content contains at least one @key and has no (url)/[ref]/{attrs} tail. A leading + signals an integral/in-text citation. Items are ;-separated; each may carry a -/+ prefix and an optional , locator. The @key and the -/+ per-item markers are scoped distinctly, analogous to @mention but inside the citation bracket.

patterns.name: entity.name.citation.carve
patterns.comment: Match the whole citation bracket [+?...@key...] that is NOT followed by (, [, or { (which would make it a link, ref-link, or span). A lookahead for @ inside the brackets discriminates from plain spans and footnote refs.
Optional -/+ per-item modifier immediately before the @key
patterns.name: keyword.control.citation.modifier.carve

patterns.comment: @key: citation key with allowed charset [A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_:.#$%&+?<>~/-]*
patterns.name: variable.parameter.citation.key.carve

patterns.comment: Semicolon item separator
patterns.name: keyword.control.separator.citation.carve

code-callouts.comment: CodeCallout markers: <N> where N is one or more digits. Leading form at the start of a callout annotation line (^<N> prose); trailing form inside fenced-code body lines (code  <N>). Both share the same scope.

patterns.comment: Leading callout annotation line: <N> at the very start (with optional leading whitespace), followed by a space and annotation prose.
patterns.name: markup.callout.annotation.carve

patterns.comment: Trailing callout marker inside a code line: <N> at the end of the line (optionally preceded by whitespace).
patterns.name: markup.callout.marker.carve
meta.attributes.carve
patterns.comment: The empty / whitespace-only block is a blessed EMPTY attribute block only when it directly abuts the `]` of a span (grammar.ebnf: `[text]{}` / `[text]{ }` -> bare `<span>`). Elsewhere it is literal: on its own line (corpus 123) and after an image or link destination (corpus 75-3). The `(?<=\])` guard encodes exactly that adjacency.

patterns.name: meta.attributes.carve
patterns.comment: Strict identifier (spec PART 9 S14, corpus 122): a class/id/key may not start with a digit, so `{2=v}` stays literal text. An unquoted value may still contain dots and colons (corpus 110); a quoted value may contain braces and backslash-escaped quotes (corpus 64-3/64-9/64-11); a bare `{}` is literal (corpus 123).

The language attribute (markup-carve/carve#1114) is the one item that opens with a colon. It goes FIRST: the key rule below admits a leading colon but needs an `=` after it, so `:fr` would otherwise fall through every rule and keep only the anonymous meta scope. The lookbehind is what keeps it an ITEM: an unquoted value may itself begin with a colon (`{key=:fr}`), and that colon starts at the same offset as the value rule's match, so without the boundary the first-listed language rule would claim it.
patterns.name: entity.other.attribute-name.language.carve

patterns.comment: An unquoted value may contain dots and colons (`k=v.w`, corpus 110); consume it whole so the dot is not mistaken for a class.
patterns.name: string.unquoted.attribute.carve

patterns.comment: Closed span, like #inline-code: a match rule is line-bounded, so an unclosed opener cannot leak literal scoping into the rest of the document.
patterns.name: markup.raw.inline.literal.carve

patterns.comment: Closed span, like #inline-code: a match rule is line-bounded, so an unclosed opener cannot leak math scoping into the rest of the document. Display ($$) is tried before inline ($).
patterns.name: markup.other.math.display.carve

emphasis.comment: The bare emphasis delimiter set is `/ * _ ~ =`. Superscript and subscript are braced-only (`{^sup^}` / `{,sub,}`): a bare `^text^` or `,text,` is literal text and gets no emphasis scope, so no rule matches them here. The caret keeps its other, unrelated roles (line-start `^ ` captions, table header rowspan `^` cells, `^[...]` inline footnotes), which are matched by their own rules outside this emphasis group.

patterns.comment: Forced intraword bold (PART 9 S22). The content runs to the closing `*}`, so it may contain the delimiter.
patterns.name: markup.bold.carve

patterns.comment: Forced intraword italic (PART 9 S22). The content runs to the closing `/}`, so it may contain the delimiter (`{/a/b/}` -> a/b, corpus 01-emphasis-13).
patterns.name: markup.italic.carve

patterns.comment: Forced intraword underline (PART 9 S22). `{_path_}` (corpus 01-emphasis-12) is shape-identical to a boolean attribute block, so this rule only wins because the whole emphasis group is listed before `#attributes`.
patterns.name: markup.underline.text.carve

patterns.comment: Forced intraword strikethrough (PART 9 S22). `#critic-markup` is listed first, so an editorial substitution `{~old~>new~}` still wins; only an arrow-less `{~x~}` lands here.
patterns.name: markup.deleted.carve

comment-fence-on-marker-line.comment: A COMMENT FENCE MAY OPEN ON A LIST ITEM'S MARKER LINE (`- %%%`), and then its body is hidden exactly as it is anywhere else: spec PART 9 section 24 S2 with section 28 make a comment's body verbatim and invisible WHEREVER the fence sits, so the whole run from opener to closer is one comment and nothing after it is affected (corpus 337, markup-carve/intellij-carve#74). `#comments` cannot reach it - its begin is anchored on ^ with only whitespace allowed before the run - so the `%%%` fell through to the line-comment rule, the hidden `[r]: /url` came back as live syntax, and the REAL closer was then taken for an opener and swallowed every block after the item. Fixed in every sibling already: markup-carve/carve-grammars#243 and #244, markup-carve/vscode-carve#113. THE MARKER IS MATCHED HERE RATHER THAN LEFT TO `#lists`, for the reason `#block-quote-on-marker-line` gives beside it: the sibling grammars reach this line with a \G-anchored rule scoped to the list item's own container, and this grammar has no container model, so a top-level \G rule would fire after any match that ends on whitespace. The marker keeps its own list scopes through the captures and only the fence run and its body are comment - tree-sitter-carve's split, with the `fenced_comment_block` inside `list_item_content` beside the `list_marker_*` rather than over it. The end has TWO branches. The first is the ordinary closer, INDENTED because it sits at the item's content column. The second is a zero-width container boundary: the first line that does not sit PAST the opener's own indent ends the item and with it the open fence, so corpus 326-6 (`- %%%` / `c` / `%%%` / `tail`) keeps `c` VISIBLE. Without it an unclosed opener would run to end of document. IT IS THE OPENER'S INDENT AND NOT COLUMN 0, which is where the sibling grammars stop: written `^(?=[^ \t\n])` the boundary only fires at column 0, so a fence on a NESTED item's marker line (`- outer` / `  - %%%` / `  - sibling`) swallowed its own sibling, which the engine renders as an ordinary second item. The indent is capture 1, so `^(?!\1[ \t])` reconstructs the item's own column from the marker line rather than assuming the document's. markup-carve/vscode-carve#127 has the same gap and cannot express this - its rule is \G-anchored and captures no indent. A TAB BETWEEN THE MARKER AND THE OPENER used to fall through: the opener was matched flush against the prefix, so `- \t> q` and `- \t%%%` took no scope even though the engine opens the block on both. The `[ \t]*` here is the same one the rest of the marker-line family carries. It is only the indent past the marker's own separator, which is still a literal space - `-\t> q` remains a paragraph.

comment-fence-on-quote-marker-line.comment: THE SAME RULE AT A BLOCK-QUOTE MARKER (`> %%%`): section 24 S2 with section 28 hide a comment's body WHEREVER the fence sits, and corpus 70 pins the spelling - `> q` / `> %%%` / `> x` / `> %%%` / `> body` renders the quote with `q` and `body` only. This grammar scoped both `%%%` runs as trailing LINE comments and left the hidden `[r]: /url` between them as live quote content (markup-carve/intellij-carve#74). Fixed in every sibling: markup-carve/carve-grammars#245 and #246, markup-carve/vscode-carve#115. Reached from `#block-quotes`, from BOTH of its rules, so a quote that opened on a list item's own marker line carries it too. Anchored on \G because the quote's own begin has already consumed the marker, so ^ can never match again on that line, and vscode-textmate resets \G on every following line so this can never open one. The guard admits `>` as well as whitespace because the two quote rules leave \G one character apart - the line-anchored one consumes the separator space, the marker-line one leaves it to the content - and a `%` can never be glued to a `>` in any case, since a quote marker is only a marker when a space or a line end follows it. Capture 1 is the run of FURTHER markers, so a fence opened at `> > ` is closed at `> > ` and not at `> `; capture 2 is the fence, repeated in the closer so the width matches exactly. The end's second branch is a zero-width quote boundary: an UNMARKED line is where the quote can end, and the engine degrades an unclosed opener to a line comment rather than hiding anything.
comment-fence-on-quote-marker-line.name: comment.block.carve

patterns.comment: A BLOCK OPENER MAY SIT ON A LIST ITEM'S OWN MARKER LINE, and it opens the block there. Measured against the engine bundled in this plugin: `- # h`, `- [x] # h`, `1. # h` and `- - # h` all render the heading INSIDE the item, and `- ---`, `- [ ] ---`, `1. ---` render an `<hr>` inside it. `#block-quotes` and `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` already carry this shape for `>` and `%%%` (markup-carve/intellij-carve#73, #74). The rule here is the same shape for another line-anchored block opener, added with its siblings rather than one spelling at a time - this family has come back a spelling at a time in every grammar in the org. THE MARKER PREFIX IS CHARACTER FOR CHARACTER the one those two rules use, so all of them accept and reject the same marker forms: every separator is a literal space, and an ATTRIBUTE-GLUED marker (`-{#x} # h`) is not covered, because the block's width is not whitespace. The marker keeps its own list scopes and NOTHING ELSE - the block's scopes start past it, which is the split `#block-quotes` makes with its `contentName` and the one tree-sitter-carve models, with the block inside `list_item_content` beside the `list_marker_*` rather than over it. A `match` rule has no `contentName`, so the payload is a capture group carrying the block scope with its parts captured inside it. The payload here is `#headings`, whose own rule is anchored on ^ and so can never reach past a marker: `- [x] # h` left `# h` with NO heading scope at all, while the `>` on the line beside it in the same corpus document kept its quote scope. That asymmetry is what made the gap visible (markup-carve/intellij-carve#77). Capture 10 carries the same `#trailing-comment` sub-pattern as the line-anchored rule, so `- # h %% c` still ends in a comment. THE MARKER'S OWN SEPARATOR IS A LITERAL SPACE and any further indent before the payload is not: measured, `-\t# h` is a PARAGRAPH in the engine while `- \t# h` is a heading inside the item, because the tab there is content indent rather than the marker's separator. So the prefix admits spaces only and a `[ \t]*` sits between it and the payload.

A BLOCK OPENER MAY SIT ON A LIST ITEM'S OWN MARKER LINE, and it opens the block there. Measured against the engine bundled in this plugin: `- # h`, `- [x] # h`, `1. # h` and `- - # h` all render the heading INSIDE the item, and `- ---`, `- [ ] ---`, `1. ---` render an `<hr>` inside it. `#block-quotes` and `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` already carry this shape for `>` and `%%%` (markup-carve/intellij-carve#73, #74). The rule here is the same shape for another line-anchored block opener, added with its siblings rather than one spelling at a time - this family has come back a spelling at a time in every grammar in the org. THE MARKER PREFIX IS CHARACTER FOR CHARACTER the one those two rules use, so all of them accept and reject the same marker forms: every separator is a literal space, and an ATTRIBUTE-GLUED marker (`-{#x} # h`) is not covered, because the block's width is not whitespace. The marker keeps its own list scopes and NOTHING ELSE - the block's scopes start past it, which is the split `#block-quotes` makes with its `contentName` and the one tree-sitter-carve models, with the block inside `list_item_content` beside the `list_marker_*` rather than over it. A `match` rule has no `contentName`, so the payload is a capture group carrying the block scope with its parts captured inside it. The payload here is `#thematic-break`. Its own rule requires the run to be the WHOLE line, so on a marker line the `---` fell through to `#smart-typography` and came out as an em dash - a `constant.character.entity` scope on something the engine renders as `<hr>` (markup-carve/intellij-carve#77). The run is the same three characters the line-anchored rule accepts (`---`, `***`, `___`) and, like it, there is no spaced form: `- - -` is nested lists in the engine, not a break, so admitting a spaced run here would colour a list as a rule. THE MARKER'S OWN SEPARATOR IS A LITERAL SPACE and any further indent before the payload is not: measured, `-\t# h` is a PARAGRAPH in the engine while `- \t# h` is a heading inside the item, because the tab there is content indent rather than the marker's separator. So the prefix admits spaces only and a `[ \t]*` sits between it and the payload.

A BLOCK OPENER MAY SIT ON A LIST ITEM'S OWN MARKER LINE. `#block-quotes`, `#comment-fence-on-marker-line`, `#heading-on-marker-line`, `#thematic-break-on-marker-line`, `#divs` and the `::` term rule all carry that shape already (markup-carve/intellij-carve#73, #74, #77). These are the last two members of the family and the only MULTI-LINE ones (markup-carve/intellij-carve#80). THE MARKER PREFIX IS CHARACTER FOR CHARACTER the one the other six use, so the whole family accepts and rejects the same marker forms: the marker's own separator is a literal space, further indent before the opener may be a tab, and an attribute-glued marker (`-{#x} ```js`) is not covered because the block's width is not whitespace. The marker keeps its own list scopes and nothing else. Measured against the engine bundled in this plugin: `- ```js` / `  code` / `  ``` ` renders the `<pre><code>` INSIDE the item, at every marker spelling, and `- ~~~` does the same. `#code-blocks` cannot reach it - its begin is anchored on ^ with no leading whitespace at all - so the whole line fell through and the fence took no scope. THE END HAS TWO BRANCHES, the split markup-carve/intellij-carve#74 and #76 worked out for the comment fence. The first is the ordinary closer, INDENTED, because it sits at the item's content column and `#code-blocks`'s own closer is column-0 only. The second is a zero-width container boundary: the first line that does not sit PAST the opener's own indent ends the item and the fence with it. IT IS THE OPENER'S INDENT AND NOT COLUMN 0 - capture 1 reconstructs the item's own column, so a fence on a NESTED item's marker line does not swallow its own sibling. Without the second branch an unclosed opener would run to the end of the document, which is what `#code-blocks` correctly does at the TOP level (markup-carve/intellij-carve#81) and what the engine does NOT do here: it ends the block with the item. The closer branch is `#code-blocks`'s own closer with an indent in front, deliberately including its looseness about the fence character, so the two rules stay one rule rather than drifting apart. The closer line carries the block scope through endCaptures 0, so it reads the same as the line-anchored rule; the second branch is zero-width, so naming capture 0 costs nothing there.

table-row-cells.comment: The inside of a table row: the pipes, the header and span markers, and every inline that may appear in a cell. Factored out of `#tables`'s row rule so `#table-row-on-marker-line` shares it rather than carrying a second copy - one production with two spellings is the defect markup-carve/carve#755 keeps recording, and a cell inline added to one list and not the other is exactly how it shows up.

These are the last two members of the family and the only MULTI-LINE ones (markup-carve/intellij-carve#80). THE MARKER PREFIX IS CHARACTER FOR CHARACTER the one the other six use, so the whole family accepts and rejects the same marker forms: the marker's own separator is a literal space, further indent before the opener may be a tab, and an attribute-glued marker (`-{#x} ```js`) is not covered because the block's width is not whitespace. The marker keeps its own list scopes and nothing else. Measured: `- |= a |` renders the `<table>` INSIDE the item, with rows on the following lines joining it at the item's content column. `#tables`'s row rule is anchored on ^, so the first row - the one on the marker line - took no table scope while every row under it did. NO CONTAINER BOUNDARY IS NEEDED HERE, unlike the code fence beside it: a table row is a ONE-LINE begin/end (`end` is `$`), so there is nothing to run away. The rows that follow are already matched by `#tables`, whose `^(?=\s*\|)` admits their indent. Only the content past the marker is `contentName`d as the row.
